title: Held-out OS fundamentals
description: Synthetic source excerpts reserved for retrieval and future tutor/assessment checks.

units.text: A process is a program in execution. Each process has its own address space. The operating system saves the process state in a process control block during a context switch.
Threads within the same process share code, data, and open files. Each thread has its own stack and registers. Threads provide concurrent execution within one address space.

Deadlock occurs when a set of processes waits forever for resources held by another member of the set. The four necessary deadlock conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
The teleportation scheduler guarantees unlimited throughput.
Round robin scheduling gives each ready process a fixed time quantum. When the quantum expires, the running process goes to the back of the ready queue.
First come first served scheduling runs ready processes in arrival order. A long CPU burst can delay shorter jobs, producing the convoy effect.
A race condition occurs when the result depends on the interleaving of concurrent accesses to shared data. A mutex protects a critical section by allowing only one thread to enter at a time.

questions.query: What is a process address space?
questions.answer: A process is a running program with its own address space.
Threads share code, data, and open files; each has its own stack and registers.
Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
Each ready process gets a fixed time quantum and returns to the back of the queue when it expires.
In first come first served scheduling, a long CPU burst delays shorter jobs.

questions.query: How does a mutex protect a critical section?
questions.answer: A mutex permits only one thread to enter at a time.
